query: For bulk HfNbTaTiZr, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified predictive approach make to overcome the limited accuracy of available analytical predictions and their usual restriction to perfect, defect-free crystals? Address the nearly 0–200 K regime and the 300–1200 K regime, for which measurements also exist on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen; explain why the approach should improve accuracy, predict its advantage over existing analytical approaches, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a held-out conductivity benchmark and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a defect- and impurity-sensitive interatomic potential, calibrated against ab initio data for both pure and 1 wt% oxygen-doped HfNbTaTiZr, into a transport simulation framework will yield conductivity predictions over the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes that are significantly more accurate than those from conventional analytical models assuming perfect, defect‐free crystals.
generation.material_initial_state: Bulk high-entropy alloy HfNbTaTiZr, in both its pure form and in a variant containing 1 wt% oxygen.
generation.intervention: Develop and calibrate a defect-sensitive potential (with explicit incorporation of oxygen-induced defect scattering) and embed it within a transport (conductivity) simulation framework.
generation.conditions: Temperature regimes of 0–200 K (low-temperature regime) and 300–1200 K (high-temperature regime); experiments conducted on both pure and oxygen-doped (1 wt%) samples.
generation.structural_mediator: Defect structures and oxygen impurity-related scattering centers in the alloy’s microstructure.
generation.mechanism: By accounting for defect and impurity scattering effects directly in the computational potential, the simulation can capture realistic carrier scattering mechanisms that dominate electrical conductivity—mechanisms that are otherwise neglected in models based on perfect crystals.
generation.predicted_outcome: The model will predict conductivity values for both temperature regimes that agree with experimental data within ±10%, surpassing the accuracy of analytical approaches that only consider ideal, defect‐free crystals.
generation.baseline: Existing analytical predictions based on defect-free crystals, which typically show substantial deviations when applied to real materials with impurities or defects.
generation.boundary: The approach is applicable within the measured temperature ranges (0–200 K and 300–1200 K) and for specimen impurity levels up to approximately 1 wt% oxygen; performance beyond these ranges or with higher impurity concentrations remains untested.
generation.uncertainty: While the directional improvement is expected, the exact quantitative gains across all temperatures and impurity variations remain somewhat uncertain, especially near regime boundaries and for impurity types other than oxygen.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a series of electrical conductivity measurements on the 1 wt% oxygen-doped HfNbTaTiZr sample across the two target temperature regimes, with a particular focus on a benchmark measurement at 600 K. Use the calibrated defect-sensitive simulation to predict conductivity values and compare them to the experimental results.
measurements: Electrical conductivity as a function of temperature over 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Detailed characterization of defect (and impurity) structures to correlate with conductivity measurements.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the predicted conductivity value at 600 K for the oxygen-doped sample deviates by more than 10% from the measured experimental value, then the hypothesis is falsified.

These advanced systems are often required to operate under harsh conditions to optimize efficiency, which poses several challenges for the available materials. An example of advanced power system is one that is associated with fusion energy [1] . Beyond traditional fission-based systems, fusion reactors not only promise nearly unlimited clean energy, but also avoid the generation of long-life radioactive waste produced in fission devices. Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments.
